title: Introduction to Human-Building Interaction (HBI): Interfacing HCI with Architecture and Urban Design
target_construct: Human-Building Interaction (HBI) as an interdisciplinary domain, its mission, vision, and scope, and a framework for research and design in built environments

findings.consequent: an interdisciplinary domain of research interfacing Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) with Architecture and Urban Design
examines the involvement of HCI in studying and steering the evolution of built environments
produces knowledge and practical guidelines by experimenting novel design instances that combine architecture and digital interaction
focuses on human values, needs, and priorities in addressing people's interactions with 'smart' environments, contrasting with the 'Smart Agenda's' emphasis on efficiency, cost, and sustainability
are concerned with the relations between human experiences, interactivity, and the design of built environments, potentially incorporating computing
extends to urban experiences, mobility, autonomous vehicles, urban delivery robots, and their interaction with humans as trans-scalar actors of mobility

are constructions of physical elements that create and protect space, with physical and spatial aspects carrying social value; designing HBI involves providing interactive opportunities for people to shape these physical, spatial, and social impacts
introduces new methodological requirements for built environments, distinct from artifacts, and addresses this gap on four fronts

components.name: Three Coordinates of HBI Research
components.description: People, Built Environment, and Computing, reflecting the three relevant entities for HBI questions.

components.name: Three Interrelated Dimensions of HBI Research
components.description: Physical (or physical-material), Social (or social-cultural), and Spatial (or spatial-configurational), specifying directions for HBI research.

components.name: Four Fronts for HBI Methodological Development
components.description: 1. Developing and re-appropriating frameworks, concepts, vocabularies, and discourses within architecture and urban design. 2. Examining how existing user research methods from HCI and other disciplines can be reappropriated. 3. Developing new and novel methods for emerging phenomena like AI and new forms of interactivity in built environments. 4. Reconciling differences in methods, terminology, and approaches between Architecture and HCI.

recommended_use: To provide a framework to understand, compare, and relate converging research efforts from HCI and Architecture in envisioning and shaping the future of living; to inform design researchers about the effectiveness of design interventions; to contribute to the generalized framework of HBI (design heuristics, strong concepts, evaluation methods); to exemplify rigor in HBI methodological and conceptual contributions and opportunities for grounded experiment-based HBI studies; to ignite discussions for a foundation for future HBI research and design; to help situate HBI among HCI sub-domains and potentially lead to independent scientific events.
limitations: HBI studies at the scope of urban settings remain lacking in the special issue.

paper_metadata.title: Introduction to Human-Building Interaction (HBI)
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Buildings and urban spaces increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence and new forms of interactivity, raising a wide span of research questions about the future of human experiences with, and within, built environments. We call this emerging area Human-Building Interaction (HBI) and introduce it as an interdisciplinary domain of research interfacing Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) with Architecture and Urban Design. HBI seeks to examine the involvement of HCI in studying and steering the evolution of built environments. Therefore, we need to ask foundational questions such as the following: what are the specific attributes of built environments that HCI researchers should take into account when shifting attention and scale from “artefacts” to “environments”? Are architecture and interaction design methods and processes compatible? Concretely, how can a team of interaction designers bring their tools to an architectural project, and collaborate with other stakeholders? Can and will architecture change the theory and practice of HCI? Furthermore, research in HBI should produce knowledge and practical guidelines by experimenting novel design instances that combine architecture and digital interaction. The primary aim of this article is to specify the mission, vision, and scope of research in HBI. As the introductory article to the TOCHI special issue, it also provides a summary of published manuscripts and describes their collective contribution to the development of this field.

crossref_authors.name: Elizabeth F. Churchill
